## ch:EYE-DRIFT - Eye drift points to a shared neural drive

Source file: `content/chapters/04-eye-drift.md`

Purpose: Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]

Prerequisites: ch:PERSISTENCE, ch:MEMORY-DYNAMICS

Sidecar sections: From stored eye position to muscle action, The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time, A fitted model links movement to firing rate, A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes, The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone, Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance

> A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p5 sha256 fd9fd365a43ffa239f2316b9104d766f576a9e7739754f0fd417dd1ba3c16e72 -->
p5, lines 5-5; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p3; next: p7

> Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. The cell fires where this function exceeds a threshold. The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.[^p3-question]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p7 sha256 94f66f9b0d8db8b88fabb359bc34b53d9b8be9d958461329ef264b77ecfed540 -->
p7, lines 7-7; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p5; next: p9

> We begin on a track, where a field starts at an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold. Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes.

### Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields Location: line 11, anchor `sec:PLACE-GP` First content kind: `prose` Opening passage line: 13 Closing passage line: 74 Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`): p13, lines 13-13; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p9; next: p15 > To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. p15, lines 15-15; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p13; next: p22 > A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector. For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, p22, lines 22-22; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p15; next: p24 > The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian. For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model] p24, lines 24-24; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p22; next: p26 > Three assumptions have different jobs: p26, lines 26-26; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p24; next: p27 > [**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation. It does not say that a particular map is flat. p27, lines 27-27; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p26; next: p28 > [**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$. It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. p28, lines 28-28; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p27; next: p30 > [**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives. Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. p30, lines 30-30; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p28; next: p32 > A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. p32, lines 32-32; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p30; next: p40 > Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, p40, lines 40-40; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p32; next: p42 > Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model] p42, lines 42-42; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p40; next: p48 > The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is p48, lines 48-48; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p42; next: p50 > Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions. p50, lines 50-50; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p48; next: p57 > For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives p57, lines 57-57; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p50; next: p64 > The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale p64, lines 64-64; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p57; next: p66 > Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] p66, lines 66-66; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p64; next: p68 > A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$. p68, lines 68-68; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p66; next: p72 >
p72, lines 72-72; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p68; next: p74 >
p74, lines 74-74; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p72; next: p78 > Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13). > The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence. A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent.

> A model can fit field volumes and still place activity incorrectly within those volumes. Slicing the map tests that internal spatial structure.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p177 sha256 7fcf2dfddf9b5536a5156f479958372adf7f807b8bf2cec9a245d5fda588393c -->
p177, lines 177-177; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p175; next: p179

> Restrict a Gaussian field to a straight line $x=x_0+tv$. At any chosen values $t_1,\ldots,t_n$, its values are a subset of the original jointly Gaussian values. They therefore remain jointly Gaussian. Along the line the covariance is $C((t-t')v)$; for a unit direction in an isotropic field it has the same local length scale $\sigma$. The same argument applies to a flat plane. First slicing and then thresholding gives the same active portions as thresholding and then slicing.[^p3-slices-source]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p179 sha256 92a306ecd5eec60105b9f9987ed8da5e18e423dd44d473ac381bb4733ac32c70 -->
p179, lines 179-179; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p177; next: p181

> Thus a line through a 2D or 3D map has the one dimensional excursion prediction, and a plane through a 3D map has the two dimensional prediction. The field being counted is now a connected active interval or patch in that slice. One 3D component can be missed, cut into multiple pieces, or intersect several slices.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p181 sha256 8288d06f0fd3bc7d03fe0a33a62b0c92937d4d02dd69a3155ac75dc3cf9f1a7d -->
p181, lines 181-181; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p179; next: p183

> The sampling rule matters. Choosing one original field uniformly and cutting through its centre is different from choosing lines uniformly through space. Large fields are more likely to be hit by a spatially sampled line, and most hits pass away from their centres. The Gaussian restriction argument describes excursions along the sampled line. The radius distribution for fields counted once each cannot be used directly as the distribution of lengths observed along a line. In the high peak picture, an isotropic $d$ dimensional field has a radius of order $\sigma/q$; converting this same radius into $d$ dimensional size and then cutting it requires both hit probability and cut position.

> Return to the [crossing integral](ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice) and retain only slopes between $v$ and $v+dv$. Their contribution is proportional to $v p_{z'}(v)dv$. Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing:

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p202 sha256 22f7985306579c6dae07453b788a543b49a4a30b7302abc69192d261fc39dc1c -->
p202, lines 202-202; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p194; next: p206

> The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of $q$ under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation. Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is $av$, so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.[^p3-slope-source]

## ch:PLACE-TESTS - Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation

## ch:SYNTHESIS - Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests

Source file: `content/chapters/06-synthesis.md`

Purpose: A model can explain the shape of a neural code without explaining how that code is maintained. It can also explain fluctuations inside a circuit without uniquely locating the source of a measured behavior. > **Place-field statistics:** A model that matches one distribution may have enough adjustable parameters to do so for several different reasons. > **Eye drift:** The eye paper calibrates a movement-to-firing relationship, inverts it, and compares the resulting single-neuron displacement predictions with measured displacement. <!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p97 sha256 fb7c417261e9f39abe25e9c54a0513aab6392fbaa5858b11b366f012db803015 -->
p97, lines 97-97; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p95; next: p99

> **Integrating movement:** The eye-position account begins with Seung's line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete's earlier grid-cell study examines [**path integration**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, updating a position estimate from movement. In its model, velocity drives recurrent population activity, and errors accumulate in the position estimate. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.[^s-attractors]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p99 sha256 246e640967b354dad7572f93f73a8a92bf512c987cd27a6e3debb2ef10642eab -->
p99, lines 99-99; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p97; next: p101

> **Storage capacity and changing synapses:** Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior; transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.[^s-extensions]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p101 sha256 35ecf69af1e00f263011e694a4578723a886e6b09ba2380aba18ba9c4469a0de -->
p101, lines 101-101; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p99; next: p103

> **Recordings from larger environments:** For place fields, Eliav and colleagues' long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues' large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.[^s-place-data]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p103 sha256 b7a1cc065d5c2ad942ab5ecd1ca0052ab0188751d98e397ce4eb9886c4bc39e2 -->
p103, lines 103-103; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p101; next: p105

> **Connectivity and learning:** Gaussian spatial statistics do not identify a unique pattern of connections. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in [**dendrite**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s, the branching input structures of neurons, can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model's success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.[^s-wiring]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p105 sha256 0ff5e5f6c91d8070a3687305852c8017a4c42373f6fa5489195fa9f6d61ba483 -->
p105, lines 105-105; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p103; next: p109

> **Benefits for perception:** The source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.[^s-acuity]
